title: Where is your money right now?
principle: Stock and credit are cash you can't spend. Limit both.

screens.text: Let me start with a story from Uttar Pradesh. A cane farmer, Piyush Kumar, sold his crop to a sugar mill, and by May 2019 the mill owed him ₹80,000. The law says a mill paying after 14 days must add interest, yet by September he still hadn't been paid.

screens.prompt: He had sold his whole crop. What do you think four months of waiting did to him?

options.label: Not much. The money was safe

screens.why: His own bills didn't wait. Piyush owed more than ₹1 lakh on a bank loan, and the bank sent him a notice. He had sold his crop and still had nothing to pay with, and he told a reporter he no longer grows cane on his 30 acres.

screens.title: Yours, but stuck
screens.text: Now you know what happened, but notice that Piyush had earned his ₹80,000. It just wasn't in his hands while his own bills carried on. He wasn't alone either: in September 2019, UP's mills owed cane farmers ₹6,480 crore for cane they had already grown and sold.

screens.title: Your money's trip
screens.text: Think of your money going on a trip. It leaves when you pay your supplier, waits on your shelf as stock, then waits with a customer who owes you, and finally comes home. Those days away are your cash conversion cycle, and supplier credit makes the trip start later.

screens.prompt: Let's try one. Pay for goods today, sell them 20 days later, get paid 30 days after that. How long is your cash away?
screens.why: Exactly. Your money spends 20 days on the shelf, then 30 more waiting for the buyer, so 20 + 30 = 50 days away. That's your cash conversion cycle.

wrong.a: That's only the first stop, the 20 days on the shelf. After the sale, the buyer keeps your money for 30 more days, so it's away for 20 + 30 = 50 days.
wrong.b: I see what you did: you counted the 30 days the buyer took. But your money had already sat on the shelf for 20 days before that, so the trip is 50 days.

screens.prompt: The mill kept Piyush's money for four months, not 14 days. Who really paid for that wait?

options.label: Nobody. The money was coming anyway

screens.why: Right. The mill used his ₹80,000 for free, while his own loan kept charging him interest. That's the thing to remember: a customer who pays late is borrowing your money for free, and if you've borrowed to fill the gap, you're the one paying the interest.

wrong.a: That's what the law says should happen, but farmers weren't getting that interest. Meanwhile, Piyush's own loan kept growing, so he paid for the wait.
wrong.c: The money was coming, but late money still costs something. While he waited, his loan kept charging interest and the bank sent him a notice.

screens.title: From their story to yours
screens.text: You don't have to grow cane to get stuck like Piyush. Any business that sells on credit is lending its money to customers, often without noticing. So let's look at yours. Say you run a small printing press that sells letterheads and visiting cards to offices.

screens.prompt: Offices order ₹20,000 of printing from you every day and pay 60 days later. How much of your money are they holding?
screens.why: Well done. Every day ₹20,000 of new bills joins the pile, and each one stays for 60 days, so ₹20,000 × 60 = ₹12 lakh is always out. That's money you've earned and can't spend.

wrong.a: I see what you did: the zeros slipped. ₹20,000 × 60 is ₹12,00,000, which is ₹12 lakh.
wrong.b: That's 30 days of bills. Your offices take 60, so ₹20,000 × 60 = ₹12 lakh is out.

screens.prompt: Offices order ₹20,000 a day. If new customers pay in 30 days instead of 60, how much cash comes home?
screens.why: Exactly. At 30 days, ₹20,000 × 30 = ₹6 lakh stays out, so the other ₹6 lakh comes home. If you'd otherwise borrow that ₹6 lakh at 12% a year, you've just saved ₹72,000 a year without selling one more card.

wrong.b: Multiply sales a day by the days: ₹20,000 × 30 = ₹6 lakh still out. Before it was ₹12 lakh, so ₹6 lakh comes home.
wrong.c: Not all of it. Customers still take 30 days, so ₹6 lakh stays out, and the other ₹6 lakh comes home.

screens.prompt: You also keep ₹4 lakh of paper and ink, using ₹10,000 a day. Keep just 8 days' worth, and how much cash comes free?
screens.why: Well done. Right now ₹4 lakh is 40 days of paper. 8 days needs only 8 × ₹10,000 = ₹80,000, so ₹4,00,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹3,20,000 comes free. Stock on your shelf is cash on its trip too.

wrong.a: That's what 8 days of paper costs, which is what you'd keep. Take it away from the ₹4 lakh you hold now, and ₹3,20,000 comes free.
wrong.c: I see what you did: you took off one day's ₹10,000. But 8 days of paper is 8 × ₹10,000 = ₹80,000, so ₹3,20,000 comes free.

screens.prompt: I'll show you seven moves for your press. For each one, tell me: does it bring cash home sooner, or keep it away longer?

items.text: Ask 30% up front on big orders
Buy 3 months of paper for a bulk discount
Give a new client 90 days to pay
Get 30 days to pay your paper supplier
Keep every paper type in every colour
Offer 2% off for payment in 7 days

screens.why: Advances, quick payment, clearing old stock and more time from your supplier all shorten your money's trip. Long credit and big piles of stock make it longer. Notice that some moves have a price, though: the 2% discount frees cash by giving up 2%.

screens.setup: Then a big chance arrives. A hotel group orders ₹10 lakh of menus, brochures and cards, and wants 120 days to pay. Paper and wages cost ₹7 lakh now, and you have ₹4 lakh.
screens.question: How do you take this order without freezing all your cash?

options.label: Take it, and borrow the ₹3 lakh gap
options.outcome: You borrow ₹3 lakh and wait four months to be paid. Your paper supplier starts chasing you, and other jobs slow down because you can't buy paper.
options.why: ₹7 lakh was tied up in one order for four months, and ₹3 lakh of it was borrowed, so like Piyush, you paid interest while a buyer held your money.
options.better: Ask for an advance and shorter terms first.

options.label: Take it with 40% up front, rest in 45 days
options.outcome: Their ₹4 lakh advance plus your ₹4 lakh covers the ₹7 lakh of costs, and the other ₹6 lakh arrives in 45 days, not 120.
options.why: Well played. You cut both how much cash you put in and how long you waited. If you're a registered micro or small business, the law backs you too: a buyer that pays you after 45 days can't claim that cost against its tax until it pays.

options.label: Turn it down. It's too big for me
options.outcome: Your cash stays safe, but you miss the ₹3 lakh profit this order would have left you on better terms.
options.why: The order was fine. It was the terms that were the problem.
options.better: Change the terms before you walk away.

screens.text: Money that customers owe you is a ___ you give. The days your cash is away are your cash conversion ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Piyush had sold his crop, so on paper he was owed ₹80,000, but while the mill held it, his own loan kept growing. Know how long your money is away, and keep that trip short.

summary: Your cash conversion cycle is the days your money is away: on your shelf, then with customers, less the time suppliers give you.
Cash stuck = sales a day × days customers take to pay. It's a loan you give, with no interest.
Cut days of credit and days of stock, and cash comes home.

cards.front: What do you call the days from paying for stock to getting paid by customers?
cards.back: The cash conversion cycle. Sell ₹10,000 a day with 45 days of credit, and ₹10,000 × 45 = ₹4,50,000 is stuck.

cards.front: A big buyer wants 90 days. You're a small registered maker. Ask for:
cards.back: Buyers who pay small makers after 45 days lose a tax deduction until they pay.
